questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.topic: A statute that recognised organisation and limited a stoppage
questions.learningObjective: Explain how the labour statute protected organisation and restricted stoppage
questions.stem: Log entry, 6 March: the men in our mill have won a vote to be represented by their own union. The new federal statute made that right real and also ruled out certain kinds of stoppage. Explain how the statute managed both.

answer.exemplar: The statute gave workers the right to self-organise, to bargain through representatives of their own choosing, and to select those representatives by secret vote. At the same time it made certain stoppages unlawful, such as a stoppage aimed at forcing recognition of a union or one aimed at a dispute between two unions, so that the choice to organise had to be made without compulsion. The law thus protected the choice to organise while removing the pressure tactics that made such a choice meaningless.

questions.explanation: The statute protected organisation and gave a board power to enforce it, while banning particular stoppages so force could not replace legal bargaining. Reading it as a simple ban on striking misses the pairing.
questions.hint: Name both the right granted and the stoppages barred.

answer.exemplar: The president's own deadline passed without the senate sending the bill to him, and he chose not to press the matter further. questions.stem: Log entry, 2 May: why did the designers give five permanent members a blocking vote, and what did that arrangement cost? Explain both halves.

answer.exemplar: The five permanent members were the states that carried the organisation through the war and that could not be expected to join a body in which they might be outvoted by a hostile majority, so each was given a veto over substantive decisions. The cost was that a single permanent member could stop any measure it disliked, leaving the council unable to act on disputes among the great powers themselves. In practice members found a way round this by abstaining rather than vetoing, which let the council function but weakened the certainty of any decision.

The text gives each of the five a power to stop a proposal, and in the years to come the real business of this council will be to find ways to act without stopping anything at all.

questions.stem: Log entry, 25 July: this speech describes the arrangement the speaker helped build. What follows for the council's work?

options.text: Because one permanent member can stop a proposal, members will look for ways to act without using that power
Because one permanent member can stop a proposal, most decisions will be taken by the permanent five alone
options.misconception: Believes the permanent five decide everything alone

options.text: Because one permanent member can stop a proposal, the general assembly will take over the council's work
options.misconception: Thinks the assembly will take over the council's work

options.text: Because one permanent member can stop a proposal, the permanent members will rarely disagree among themselves
options.misconception: Believes the permanent members never disagree

questions.explanation: The speech treats the veto as a power to be avoided rather than used, pointing to a council that acts by agreement among the permanent members. Believing the five would decide everything alone misreads it.
questions.hint: The speaker calls the power one to avoid.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.topic: A statute that recognised organisation and limited a stoppage
questions.learningObjective: Explain where the statute drew the line between lawful and unlawful stoppage
questions.stem: Log entry, 31 July: explain why the statute's limits on stoppages were drawn where they were, and what that says about the purpose of the law.

answer.exemplar: The statute left economic stoppages by workers over wages and conditions lawful, because the pressure of a stoppage was the means by which workers made their claims effective, but it made stoppages aimed at forcing recognition of a union or resolving a dispute between two unions unlawful, because those forms of pressure were used to bypass the choice the law protected. The line therefore distinguishes the use of stoppage to bargain from its use to compel a decision the law had already assigned to a lawful process, and it shows that the law's aim was to make organisation effective without making industrial peace depend on the ability to coerce.

questions.explanation: The limits separated stoppage used to bargain from stoppage used to compel recognition, so the protected choice was not undermined by force. Believing the statute aimed to end all conflict misreads the line drawn.
questions.hint: Ask what each kind of stoppage was trying to achieve.

questions.topic: A sudden attack and what it proved about the peacetime fleet
questions.learningObjective: Identify the weakness a prewar report documents most directly

stimulus.body: The report notes that the base had no adequate warning system for aircraft approaching from the north, and that the watch on the harbour was routine and carried out by men who had not been drilled for a surprise. It adds that the squadron commanders had asked repeatedly for more practice with torpedoes, and that the request had been declined for want of ammunition.

questions.stem: Log entry, 9 August: this note describes the base before the attack. Which weakness does it document most directly?

The ships were so old that their guns could not be used at all
options.misconception: Believes the guns were unusable through age

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.topic: The permanent members and the veto
questions.learningObjective: Explain how the blocking vote worked and was avoided in practice
questions.stem: Log entry, 15 August: explain how the blocking vote worked, and how members learned to act without using it.

answer.exemplar: Substantive decisions in the council required the concurring votes of the five permanent members, so a single one of them could stop a proposal outright. That arrangement meant the great powers could not be outvoted by a larger majority assembled against them, which was the point of the design, but it also meant the council could be frozen on any question the five disagreed about. Members developed a practice of abstaining rather than vetoing, and of explaining that a decision taken without their formal vote was not a decision they were blocking. The practice preserved the ability of the council to act, though it weakened the certainty of any resolution it produced.

questions.explanation: The blocking vote let one permanent member stop a proposal, and abstention let the council act without the power being used. Believing the permanent members could be outvoted, or that abstention was a veto, misstates both.
questions.hint: One member could stop it; abstention was the way round.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.topic: Adding seats to a court to outlast a ruling
questions.learningObjective: Explain how institutions can change without a formal amendment
questions.stem: Log entry, 18 August: explain what the abandoned enlargement plan shows about how the constitution can be changed without an amendment.

answer.exemplar: The plan was announced with a public justification and was defeated in the legislature, so the government backed away rather than pressing it, and the practice of the court shifted as its membership changed. It is therefore a reminder that judges' interpretations of a text can move over time through appointments, retirements and changes of mind, and that a president who wanted a different constitution could not obtain it by legislation alone. The episode also shows that the political cost of a proposal can be decisive even when the proposal is formally available, which is why a threat to enlarge a court was such a powerful deterrent.

questions.explanation: The plan shows a president's effort to change the court by legislation was blocked politically, while the court's practice shifted as its membership changed. Believing change came only through amendment ignores how the bench moved.
questions.hint: One route was blocked; another ran through appointments.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.topic: A third term accepted, and later written into the constitution
questions.learningObjective: Derive the design of the term limit from a citizens' request

stimulus.body: A group of citizens asked the members of congress to fix the number of terms by law rather than by custom, noting that a rule which depends on the restraint of candidates and voters can be set aside by a single popular majority. The note adds that the fix should leave the serving president free to finish his term and that a successor should be able to inherit an unfinished one.

questions.stem: Log entry, 27 August: this note asks for a legal limit on terms. Which design does the note support?

options.text: Limit the number of times a person may be elected, letting the sitting president finish and the office pass unbroken
Fix a hard ceiling on the total years any person may serve, including the current holder
options.misconception: Believes the limit was a flat cap on years served

options.text: Leave the limit to custom but require the parties to state their candidates' intentions early
options.misconception: Believes the note wanted an early declaration, not a legal limit

options.text: Limit the number of terms but strip the vice presidency of the right to succeed
options.misconception: Thinks the note wanted the succession rule changed

questions.explanation: The note supports a limit on the number of elections, with exceptions for the sitting president and for the continuity of the office, which is how the amendment was framed. Believing it asked for a flat cap on years misreads it.
questions.hint: Elections are counted, not years served.
